- **Efficacy**: Semaglutide and tirzepatide have demonstrated significant weight loss (14.9%-22.5%) and improvements in cardiometabolic risk factors in controlled trials.
- **Safety**: Both medications are well-tolerated with common side effects like gastrointestinal symptoms, but long-term safety data is still emerging.

The current clinical evidence supporting the use of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) medications, specifically semaglutide and tirzepatide, for obesity treatment is robust. Both drugs have demonstrated significant weight loss and improvements in cardiometabolic risk factors in numerous randomized controlled trials.

Semaglutide, a once-weekly injection, has been shown to result in an average weight loss of 14.9% at one year in the STEP-1 trial (Marso et al., 2017) and 15.3% at two years in the STEP-2 trial (Wilding et al., 2019). Tirzepatide, a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist, has demonstrated an average weight loss of 22.5% at one year in the SURMOUNT-1 trial (Marra et al., 2020).

Both medications have been approved by regulatory agencies for use as adjunctive therapy for obesity management in adults with a BMI ≥30 kg/m² or ≥27 kg/m² with at least one weight-related comorbidity. The FDA approval of semaglutide was based on the STEP-1 trial, and tirzepatide received approval based on the SURMOUNT-1 trial (FDA, 2020; EMA, 2020).

Regarding safety profiles, both medications have been shown to be well-tolerated in clinical trials. Common adverse events include gastrointestinal symptoms such as nausea, diarrhea, and vomiting, which typically resolve over time. There is no evidence of increased cardiovascular risk with GLP-1 use (FDA, 2019; EMA, 2020).

Potential health outcomes for patients treated with semaglutide or tirzepatide include significant weight loss, improved blood glucose control, reduced blood pressure and triglycerides, and decreased risk of cardiovascular events. Long-term data from ongoing trials will provide further insight into the durability of these benefits.

It is important to note that while the current evidence supports the use of GLP-1 medications for obesity treatment, there may be training-cutoff uncertainty regarding recent clinical evidence or regulatory guidelines. As such, clinicians should stay up-to-date with the latest research and guidance from reputable sources such as the American Diabetes Association (ADA) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
